summary: Defines extensions to WebDAV for accessing, managing, and sharing contact information in vCard format. It gives a standard way for clients to work with address books stored on a server.

plainLanguage.summary: CardDAV adds contact books to WebDAV, the protocol used for files on the web. A server keeps each address book as a folder of contacts, and clients can create, change, search and share them over the network using ordinary web requests.

questions: what is the carddav addressbook-query report
subtitle: WebDAV extensions that let a server store and search a shared address book of vCards.

tldr.problem: Contact data was spread across several protocols such as LDAP, IMSP and ACAP, and none of them shared the access control, hierarchical layout and server-side search that WebDAV already offered for other kinds of data.
tldr.mechanism: CardDAV defines an address book collection inside a WebDAV repository, one resource per contact in vCard format, extra properties, and two reports, addressbook-query and addressbook-multiget, that the server answers.
tldr.outcome: It became the standard way for clients and servers to share address books, and it is a Proposed Standard from August 2011, updated by RFC 6764.

today: RFC 6352 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2011. It is updated by RFC 6764 and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the definition of CardDAV.

sections.title: Why CardDAV Exists
sections.content:
Address books are a key part of the personal information management tools people use for email, calendaring and instant messaging. Several protocols have been used for remote access to contact data, including the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), the Internet Message Support Protocol (IMSP) and the Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP), together with SyncML for synchronizing such data.

WebDAV (RFC 4918) offers advantages as a base for address book access. Most of them come down to a significant reduction in the costs of design, implementation, interoperability testing and deployment. The features it provides are: the ability to use several address books in a hierarchical layout; access control over individual address books and address entries through the WebDAV Access Control List extension (RFC 3744); principal collections that can be used to enumerate and query other users; server-side searching of address data, which spares a client from downloading a whole address book just to expand a name; well-defined internationalization support through WebDAV's use of XML; vCards (RFC 2426) as a well-defined address schema; and the fact that limited clients such as mobile devices already contain an HTTP stack, which makes WebDAV easier to implement than the alternatives.

The one disadvantage is the lack of change notification. Many of the alternative protocols lack it too, and the document notes that a push notification extension could easily be developed. vCard itself is a MIME directory profile for personal contact information, originally specified by the Versit consortium and standardised by the IETF as vCard 3.0. It is in widespread use in email clients and mobile devices, and a newer vCard 4 was being developed at the time, compatible with this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Contact data used several different protocols, none of them sharing the folder-like layout, access control and server-side search that web servers already offered. CardDAV builds contact books on top of WebDAV so that one server can hold them all.

sections.title: What a CardDAV Server Must Support
sections.content:
To advertise support for CardDAV, a server MUST support vCard 3 as the media type for address object resources, WebDAV Class 3, WebDAV ACL, secure transport using TLS with the certificate validation procedures of RFC 5280, ETags with the additional requirements the document sets out, and all of the address book reports defined in its Section 8. It must also advertise support for those reports on every address book collection and address object resource, through the DAV:supported-report-set property from the versioning extensions in RFC 3253.

Beyond those requirements, a server SHOULD support vCard 4 as a media type, the extended MKCOL method (RFC 5689) for creating address book collections, and the DAV:current-user-principal-URL property from RFC 5397, which gives clients a fast way to find user principals.

The XML elements live in their own namespace, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:carddav, which is reserved for this specification, its revisions and related CardDAV specifications. Implementations must not use that namespace for their own elements, and should use a namespace they control instead. Element ordering does not matter unless stated, and extension elements may be added anywhere unless stated otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: A server claiming to support CardDAV has to offer a specific baseline: vCard 3 contacts, WebDAV Class 3, access control, TLS, ETags and the search reports. It should also offer vCard 4 and a way to create new address books.

sections.title: The Address Book Data Model
sections.content:
A CardDAV address book is modelled as a WebDAV collection with a well-defined structure. Each address book collection contains a number of resources that represent address objects as its direct children, and each of those is called an address object resource. Every address object resource and every address book collection can be locked individually and can carry its own WebDAV properties.

An address object resource MUST contain a single vCard component, and the UID property of that component MUST be unique within the address book collection that holds it. Servers may support more than one primary media type, for example vCard 3.0 and vCard 4.0, and then they must accept every media type they advertise through the CARDDAV:supported-address-data property. Clients use the ordinary HTTP content negotiation behaviour to ask for one format or another. When a server cannot convert between formats it MUST report the CARDDAV:supported-address-data-conversion precondition, which is also the new precondition added to the GET method.

An address book collection appears to clients as a WebDAV collection resource with a URL, and it MUST report the DAV:collection and CARDDAV:addressbook elements in the value of its DAV:resourcetype property. Inside an address book collection there may only be address object resources and collections that are not address book collections. Collections inside an address book collection MUST NOT contain address book collections at any depth, so nesting address books inside address books is not allowed. Several address book collections MAY be children of the same collection.
sections.plainLanguage: An address book is a folder. Each contact inside it is one file holding one vCard, and each contact has an identifier that must be unique within that folder. Address books cannot be nested inside other address books.

sections.title: Creating Address Books and Contacts
sections.content:
An address book collection is created with the extended MKCOL method, with the request body setting the DAV:resourcetype property to the address book resource type. A server may restrict where address books can be created. Support for creating address books is only RECOMMENDED, because some stores support one address book per user and pre-create it, but servers and clients are strongly encouraged to support it so that users can organise their contacts into several books. The DAV:displayname property gives the book a readable name, and CARDDAV:addressbook-description gives a longer description.

Contacts are added with a PUT request aimed at a URL that does not yet exist, and the client SHOULD send the header If-None-Match: * so that it does not overwrite an existing contact by accident. Changing a contact that already exists is done with a PUT carrying the entity tag in an If-Match header. The URL of a contact is arbitrary and need not match anything in the vCard, and the file name suffix .vcf is a common convention.

The document adds preconditions for PUT, COPY and MOVE: the data must be in a media type the server supports, it must be valid for that media type, it must not reuse a UID that is already in use in the target address book or replace a resource that has a different UID, the destination of a COPY or MOVE must be a place where an address book collection can be created, and the data must not exceed the size in the CARDDAV:max-resource-size property. Servers must support non-standard vCard properties and parameters whose names start with X-, and should include a vendor identifier in their own such names.

Every address object resource MUST have a strong entity tag, returned in the ETag header of a GET response and set in the DAV:getetag property. A strong entity tag MUST NOT be returned when the stored data differs from what was submitted, so the client knows to fetch the resource again before making further changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A client creates an address book with a special MKCOL request and adds contacts with PUT requests. The entity tag on each contact is what lets two clients avoid overwriting each other's work.

sections.title: Access Control and Principal Properties
sections.content:
CardDAV servers MUST support the WebDAV ACL extension (RFC 3744), which provides a framework for an extensible set of privileges applied to collections and ordinary resources. Two properties are added for principal resources. The CARDDAV:addressbook-home-set property identifies the URL of collections that contain the address book collections owned by that principal, so a user can find their own books. The CARDDAV:principal-address property identifies the URL of the address object resource that holds the contact information for the user the principal represents.

Service discovery uses SRV records (RFC 2782). The document adds two service types: carddav for a server that uses HTTP without TLS and carddavs for one that uses HTTP with TLS, with the example records _carddav._tcp SRV 0 1 80 addressbook.example.com. and _carddavs._tcp SRV 0 1 443 addressbook.example.com.. Together with the DAV:current-user-principal-URL property, a user only has to give a client an identifier, a host name and a password: the client looks up the server with SRV, then runs an authenticated PROPFIND for the principal URL, and from there reaches the properties that point at the address books.
sections.plainLanguage: The server uses the same permission system as any other web server, so an address book can be private, shared or open. Clients find the server and the user's books through a DNS lookup and a property search.

sections.title: Searching and Fetching with Reports
sections.content:
CardDAV uses the REPORT method, which is more flexible than PROPFIND because it can involve more complex processing. It is valuable when the server holds all the information needed to answer, and answering would otherwise take the client several requests. A server MUST support the DAV:expand-property report as well as the address book reports.

The CARDDAV:addressbook-query report searches for every address object resource that matches a filter, and it is REQUIRED. The request body is a CARDDAV:addressbook-query element, the request MUST include a Depth header, and the response is a DAV:multistatus element with one DAV:response element per matching contact. The filter is a CARDDAV:filter element holding CARDDAV:prop-filter elements, one per vCard property to search. A property filter matches when a property of that type exists and satisfies the text match and parameter filter conditions, or when it does not exist and the filter asks for CARDDAV:is-not-defined. The test attribute chooses whether any or all of the conditions must match.

Text matching follows the IANA Collation Registry. Servers are REQUIRED to support the i;ascii-casemap and i;unicode-casemap collations, and MUST default to i;unicode-casemap when the client does not name one. A client can also cap the number of results with the CARDDAV:limit element. When the server truncates the result set it MUST answer with status 207 and report a status of 507 for the request URI, along with the partial results.

The CARDDAV:addressbook-multiget report, also REQUIRED, fetches named resources instead of searching. It takes a list of DAV:href elements and returns one DAV:response per resource, with an error status for any resource that could not be read. Clients use it to fetch a set of contacts whose identifiers they already know.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a search request in XML that names the contact fields to look at and the text to look for. The server does the searching and sends back the matching contacts with just the fields the client asked for.

sections.title: Guidance for Clients
sections.content:
Clients do not always need every property of a vCard, and some properties can be large, such as PHOTO or SOUND with inline content. They can therefore ask for only the items they will use, through the CARDDAV:address-data element in the reports. The limitation is that a change can only be made to the whole vCard with a PUT request: there is no way to change a few properties of one contact incrementally, so the client has to keep the full set of properties for any contact it edits.

Because address books may be shared and reachable by several clients, updates can overwrite each other. Clients SHOULD use the If-Match header with the entity tag of the data they last retrieved, so that the server rejects the write if the contact changed in the meantime. When that happens the client has to reload the contact and run its own merge or conflict resolution before writing again.

To find another user's address book, for example for sharing, the DAV:principal-property-search report from RFC 3744 can be used to search principals and return chosen properties for the matching principals. The example in the document searches the DAV:displayname property for a name, which may match several people at once, and returns the CARDDAV:addressbook-home-set of each so the client can offer them as choices.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask for only the contact fields you need, and always send the version number you last saw when you save. If the server says it changed underneath you, fetch it again and merge the two versions yourself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
HTTP transactions travel in the clear unless protection from snooping is negotiated, which is accomplished with TLS. If HTTP Basic authentication is available, the server MUST allow TLS to be used at the same time and SHOULD prevent the use of Basic authentication when TLS is not in use. Clients SHOULD use TLS whenever possible.

With the ACL extension present, WebDAV controls who can read or write any resource. Its inheritance mechanism lets resources inherit privileges from others, often a parent collection. That is what allows servers to support address books that are private, accessible only to the owner, shared with specified authenticated users, or public. When provisioning an address book of a particular type, servers MUST ensure that the correct privileges are applied at creation. Private and shared address books MUST NOT be accessible by unauthenticated users, so that their data is not automatically searched or indexed by web crawlers.

Clients SHOULD warn users when they copy or move address data from a private address book into a shared or public one, SHOULD show clearly which kind each address book is, and SHOULD warn when access privileges are changed to allow unauthenticated users in. The specification relies on the standard HTTP authentication mechanisms, which are Basic and Digest authentication and TLS with client-side certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Contacts are private, so the connection should be encrypted and the books should not be readable by anyone who has not logged in. Clients should also warn a user before a private contact list is made public.

viz.caption: THE HTTP METHODS A CARDDAV CLIENT USES

items.label: DISCOVER
items.desc: The DAV header carries 'addressbook' when the server supports CardDAV.

items.label: CREATE BOOK
items.desc: Extended MKCOL creates an address book collection.

items.label: STORE CONTACT
items.desc: Creates or updates one address object resource.

items.label: SEARCH OR FETCH
items.desc: addressbook-query searches; addressbook-multiget fetches named resources.

items.label: READ PROPERTIES
items.desc: Reads WebDAV properties such as getetag and resourcetype.

data.title: Search for contacts with the nickname me
data.code:
<C:addressbook-query xmlns:D="DAV:"
                  xmlns:C="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:carddav">
  <D:prop>
    <D:getetag/>
    <C:address-data>
      <C:prop name="VERSION"/>
      <C:prop name="UID"/>
      <C:prop name="NICKNAME"/>
      <C:prop name="EMAIL"/>
      <C:prop name="FN"/>
    </C:address-data>
  </D:prop>
  <C:filter>
    <C:prop-filter name="NICKNAME">
      <C:text-match collation="i;unicode-casemap"
                    match-type="equals">me</C:text-match>
    </C:prop-filter>
  </C:filter>
</C:addressbook-query>
